sources.news_title: Democrats Sue Trump Admin To Bar US Armed Agents From Poll Sites
Leaders Jeffries and Schumer, DCCC, DSCC, and DGA File New Lawsuit to Block Trump and Republicans’ Threats to Intimidate Voters at Polling Places
sources.text:
|  | 
| After filing a lawsuit to block Donald Trump’s threats to intimidate voters by stationing armed federal agents at polling places, House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer, DCCC Chair Suzan DelBene, DSCC Chair Kirsten Gillibrand, and DGA Chair Andy Beshear released the following statement: “We are taking strong, joint legal action to block Donald Trump’s threats to deploy federal agents, including ICE and FBI agents, to polling places this November. Sending armed federal agents into American neighborhoods to intimidate voters is not only wrong – it’s illegal and would mark a new and extremely dangerous escalation of this administration’s disregard for the rule of law and repeated attempts to rig the midterms. “We will not allow Donald Trump to attack Americans’ right to vote because he knows his cost-raising agenda is deeply unpopular and will be rejected this November. Federal law explicitly forbids voter intimidation and stationing armed federal agents at polling places. Our case is clear, and we’re confident we’ll defeat Trump in court yet again.” | 
|  |

sources.news_title: Lawsuit: Trump Threats to Send ICE, FBI to Polls Violate VRA
sources.text:
The Trump administration is violating federal law by threatening to deploy armed agents to polling places, according to a lawsuit filed this week.
The complaint points to statements made in recent months by officials at the Justice Department, Department of Homeland Security (DHS), Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), and the FBI. Those remarks, the plaintiffs say, indicate that federal agents could be sent to polling locations during the upcoming midterm elections.
In a 29-page complaint, a group of Democratic organizations led by the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC) argues that the officials’ statements serve as a “preview” of a so-called “Polling Place Policy.” The groups contend that the policy would force them to compete in elections structured unlawfully.
“Notwithstanding federal law, and the traditional sanctity afforded to polling places, the Trump Administration has made clear by word and deed over the past year that it asserts the authority to dispatch armed officers to active polling locations,” the complaint states.
The plaintiffs stop short of claiming that the administration has finalized a plan to send armed personnel to polling sites. However, they argue that even threatening such action violates the Voting Rights Act (VRA) and, in turn, the Administrative Procedure Act (APA).
“[D]ispatching armed federal agents to the polls—or even threatening to do so—is forbidden by federal law,” the lawsuit says. “This is because voters need not actually be arrested, questioned, or even approached in order for such threats to intimidate them from exercising the franchise.”
The filing continues:
For many lawful American voters, the sight of masked, armed federal agents in a polling-place parking lot is enough to send them home or make them think twice about casting a ballot at all. For many others, the mere prospect of such an encounter will keep them from heading to the polls. And because no voter can know in advance whether agents will be waiting at his or her polling place when they arrive to cast a ballot, the Polling Place Policy chills voting everywhere, not only where ICE and FBI agents actually appear.
The complaint further argues that deploying armed personnel or troops to polling places would directly violate a federal statute barring such conduct unless the presence is “necessary to repel armed enemies of the United States.”
The plaintiffs maintain that no such emergency exists. They cite President Trump’s remarks about doing “anything necessary to make sure we have honest elections” as evidence of the administration’s intentions. They also point to DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin’s statement that federal agents have authority to monitor polling sites “if there was a specific threat for them to be there.”
According to the lawsuit, those statements suggest the policy would disproportionately affect voters who are most likely to fear contact with immigration authorities, including naturalized citizens.
“The Polling Place Policy, under which armed federal officers may be sent to polls, is objectively likely to intimidate voters from voting or attempting to vote, or from urging or aiding others in voting,” the filing states. “It also threatens and coerces voters who plan to cast their ballot in person at a polling place, forcing some to abandon those plans entirely.”
The lawsuit asks a federal court to issue an injunction preventing the Trump administration from implementing the policy and to prohibit a broad range of related conduct.
Specifically, the DSCC wants a judge to bar federal law enforcement officers from “operating or carrying weapons in the vicinity of open polling places, including drop boxes, curbside voting locations, and any similar places where votes are taken, collected, received, counted, or certified during early voting periods, on election day itself.”
The plaintiffs also seek to prohibit openly carried weapons during any post-election ballot-curing period. In addition, they ask the court to prevent the government from threatening to take any of those actions.
The complaint also asks the court to declare the policy unlawful and “set aside” the measure. That language refers to a specific form of relief under the APA that can nullify and vacate an agency action.
The post ‘Chills voting everywhere’: Trump admin ‘unlawfully’ threatening to send armed ICE and FBI agents into polling places is a violation of Voting Rights Act, lawsuit says first appeared on Law & Crime.

sources.news_title: Democrats Sue Trump Administration Over Armed Agents At Midterm Polls - American Liberty News
sources.text:
Democratic leaders are taking the Trump administration to federal court over a question hanging over the midterms: Could armed ICE or FBI agents show up where Americans vote?
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and three Democratic campaign committees filed a lawsuit Wednesday seeking to block such deployments at polling places and other election sites. The complaint, filed in federal court in Washington, D.C., accuses administration officials of leaving the door open to armed agents at the polls and argues that their presence would intimidate eligible voters.
The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee and Democratic Governors Association joined the two congressional leaders as plaintiffs. Their suit names the Department of Homeland Security, Immigration and Customs Enforcement, the FBI and senior officials, including Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and FBI Director Kash Patel.
The administration has not announced a plan to station agents at polling places. DHS has said ICE is not planning operations targeting voting locations. The lawsuit argues that officials’ public comments and earlier encounters involving agents at voting sites amount to a policy that must be stopped before Election Day.
A dispute over what agents could do
At a Sept. 1 news conference, Mullin said ICE would not patrol the polls. Agents would appear only for a threat to a polling place or to serve a warrant on a person they had been tracking, according to The Guardian’s reporting.
DHS separately told Politico that ICE did not plan operations targeting polling places, while leaving open the possibility of targeted enforcement in response to an active public safety threat, The Guardian reported.
Democrats say those qualifications are precisely the problem. In their complaint, they argue that the administration has claimed authority to send armed agents to active voting sites under circumstances broader than federal law permits. The suit cites Section 11(b) of the Voting Rights Act, which prohibits voter intimidation, and a separate federal statute restricting the presence of armed federal personnel where elections are held.
Patel was pressed about the issue during Senate testimony last week. Asked whether FBI agents would go to polling sites, he said the bureau would “follow the law,” as The Hill reported. “If there’s a reason to go there because there’s been a violation of law, we will,” Patel said. “Otherwise, we won’t.”
Polling-site incidents cited in the suit
The complaint points to three ICE encounters at voting locations during this year’s primaries and runoffs. It alleges that agents appeared in a San Antonio polling-site parking lot in May, lingered outside a Simi Valley, California, vote center in June, and entered a Syracuse, New York, polling place later that month.
In the Syracuse incident, the filing says agents confronted an election worker over criticism of ICE she had posted online. The complaint quotes Onondaga County’s Republican elections commissioner saying there was “no emergency” and “no threat to public safety.” The filing does not say FBI agents have appeared at an active polling location.
The Democrats want a judge to declare the administration’s alleged policy unlawful and bar unauthorized armed-agent activity near polling places, drop boxes, curbside voting sites and locations where ballots are collected or counted. They seek protection from early voting through the period when voters can correct ballot problems after Election Day.

sources.news_title: Schumer, Jeffries sue to block federal agents at polls in November
sources.text:
Schumer, Jeffries sue to block federal agents at polls in November
Democrats say they're worried about administration comments about FBI, ICE at polls
Congressional Democratic leaders filed a lawsuit Thursday aiming to prevent the Trump administration from following through on statements that they are considering sending armed federal agents to polling places in November.
The suit, filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia by Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., the national Democratic Party and Democratic campaign groups, alleges the Trump administration plans to send agents from Immigration and Customs Enforcement and the Federal Bureau of Investigation to the polls this fall.
The complaint said doing so could intimidate countless voters into not showing up at the polls in violation of federal law and their constitutional rights.
“Notwithstanding federal law, and the traditional sanctity afforded to polling places, the Trump Administration has made clear by word and deed over the past year that it asserts the authority to dispatch armed officers to active polling locations,” the complaint said.
The complaint came after President Donald Trump said in an interview that Republicans should “take over the voting” and that voting should be nationalized.
Under the Constitution, states and Congress hold authority over federal elections, and the complaint alleges that Trump has taken numerous efforts to assert authority over federal elections he does not have.
Federal law prohibits federal or other officials from intimidating voters at the polls, but the complaint alleges the Trump administration has suggested that it intends to do just that.
“For many lawful American voters, the sight of masked, armed federal agents in a polling-place parking lot is enough to send them home or make them think twice about casting a ballot at all,” the complaint said.
The complaint said that over the past several months, both Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and White House “border czar” Tom Homan have said the Department of Homeland Security has the authority to send agents to polling places. Homan earlier this month dismissed the idea that there are plans to “sweep” polling locations.
At the Conservative Political Action Conference in March, Attorney General Todd Blanche, who was the No. 2 at DOJ at the time, said there should not be a problem with sending federal agents to the polls.
“Why is there objection to sending ICE officers to polling places?” he asked then. “Illegals can’t vote.”
Other officials, including FBI Director Kash Patel earlier this month, refused to rule out sending agents to polling places, the complaint said.
During a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing, Patel said concerns about FBI agents at polls were a “charade of lies” and said that agents had the authority to protect elections.
“Election integrity is of paramount importance. This FBI will not shy away from that effort,” Patel said.
Separately, the Justice Department has reportedly removed a manual from its website that included prohibitions on interfering with elections, the complaint said, and not established a center that it normally does to protect elections.
The complaint also accused DHS of slow-walking the release of documents about the policy in a separate Freedom of Information Act lawsuit. Although the agency identified more than 10,000 records related to the policy, the complaint said, it has tried to delay release of those documents until after the elections.
Thursday’s suit called the policy “part and parcel with various executive initiatives announced by President Trump that have sought to usurp authority for the Executive Branch to influence and ultimately control the nation’s elections.”
The suit argued the Trump administration’s actions violate the federal Voting Rights Act as well as federal administrative law. The complaint asked the judge to declare the policy unlawful and order the administration not to send any agents to polling places.
The complaint joins lawsuits brought by civil rights groups in the last several weeks seeking to block the administration from sending armed federal agents to the polls. Those suits are currently pending in D.C. federal court, but the administration has not yet filed a response to any of those complaints.
Thursday’s suit by Democrats, as well as the other two pending suits, did not ask for immediate action by the courts.
The White House did not directly respond to questions about the lawsuit, but in February, then-White House spokeswoman Karoline Leavitt denied that the president was considering allowing ICE to monitor the polls.
“That’s frankly a very silly hypothetical question,” she said then, adding, “I haven’t heard the president discuss any formal plans to put ICE outside of polling locations.”
John T. Bennett contributed to this report.

Democrats file lawsuit against Trump for threatening to send agents to polling stations
sources.text:
Democrats file lawsuit against Trump for threatening to send agents to polling stations
WASHINGTON (TNND) — Campaign organizations and leaders in the Democratic Party filed a lawsuit against the Trump administration on Wednesday over allegedly threatening to deploy federal troops to polling sites during the midterm elections.
The lawsuit was filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia. It accuses the Trump administration law enforcement of demonstrating “by word and deed that they have established a policy of permitting their armed officers to appear at active polling sites,” according to The Hill newspaper.
The Trump administration hasn’t ruled out the possibility of sending troops to the polls but says it doesn’t have formal plans to do it.
Earlier this month Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said federal agents would only be at polling places if there was a threat or to serve a warrant.
When Attorney General Todd Blanche was getting confirmed, Minnesota Democratic Sen. Amy Klobuchar asked him if he would commit to not sending armed agents to polling sites.
“Federal law has made it clear that the president does not have the authority to reply armed federal officials to election sites,” Klobuchar said. “Will you commit to following clear federal law and not deploying federal agents to polling locations?”
“I will commit to following the law,” he answered her. “Of course.”
Klobuchar said that Americans are concerned about armed agents at polling stations.
“I’m not aware of armed agents being at polling places so I’m not aware of that concern,” Blanche said. “But I will tell you [that] we will follow the law, Senator.”
